evaluation.positioning_hook: A horny, weed-smoking teen strikes a bargain with God and Satan to win the girl of his dreams, only to discover the real prize is choosing who he becomes.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and the teen-sex-comedy engine is easy to sell, but the explicit language, blasphemous setup, and abrasive humor narrow the audience. It has a clear lane with adult genre buyers and cult-comedy viewers, but not broad four-quadrant reach.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: Leo wants Vivian, prays, meets God, then gets propositioned by Satan. The bargain structure is simple to explain in one breath, and the feature stays organized around that choice.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Leo has a usable comic engine — horny, insecure, self-mythologizing, and finally capable of decency with Amanda — but he is more broad than layered for much of the script. Vivian, Amanda, Wayne, and Bruce all pop, though mostly as functions of Leo’s orbit.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a profane, cartoonish theology where God and Satan are both active, argumentative characters, and that gives it a distinct comic identity. The boldness is real, even when the execution leans on shock and repetition.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story moves through a clear weekend-to-decision structure, with the party sequence giving it a strong middle engine. It does sag into repeated temptation beats and long explanatory dialogue from Satan before the final wish sequence pays off.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea — a teenage loser negotiating with both God and Satan for love, status, and self-worth — is strange in a way that is immediately graspable. The Amanda/Vivian reversal and the final bargain give it a fresh emotional turn, even if the comic surface is very broad.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The school and party worlds are specific, vulgar, and socially legible, with enough teen hierarchy to generate scenes. But the world is mostly a container for Leo’s misadventures rather than a deeply rule-bound ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: This has a very particular register: raunchy, irreverent, cartoonish, and aggressively juvenile in a way that is hard to mistake for anything else. The tonal identity is strong, though it will be polarizing by design.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are real themes underneath the vulgarity — loneliness, desirability, disability, faith, and the difference between being wanted and being seen — but the script mostly plays them through gag structure. The Amanda ending hints at more emotional depth than the rest of the piece fully earns.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Leo/Wayne/Bruce has a workable buddy-comedy rhythm, and the Leo/Vivian/Amanda triangle gives the feature a clear relational spine. Still, most supporting characters are one-note, so the ensemble energy is more functional than generative.

lead_characters.name: Leo
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 16 in the main timeline; white/Canadian; teen stoner, socially awkward, sexually frustrated, later older man in his 90s framing the story.
lead_characters.hook: A metalhead stoner with a huge libido and a fragile ego, Leo is the kind of kid who mistakes lust for destiny and then has to live inside the consequences. He narrates his own humiliation with enough confidence to make him funny, and enough sincerity to make the eventual Amanda turn land as more than a punchline.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jason Biggs in American Pie — a horny, embarrassed, self-exposing lead who can carry humiliation comedy and still win sympathy. It also gives an actor the rare chance to play a broad comic engine that eventually pivots into genuine emotional recognition.

lead_characters.name: Amanda
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16; blind; socially isolated teen who becomes physically and emotionally transformed.
lead_characters.hook: Amanda starts as the overlooked blind girl at school, but the script gives her a sharp revenge turn once she can see and finally has social power. She is quiet, wounded, and then suddenly dangerous in a way that makes her more than the sympathetic alternative to Vivian.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Marlee Matlin in Children of a Lesser God its lasting force — a character whose vulnerability and agency are both playable, with a late-blooming power shift. It offers an actor a transformation beat that is emotionally legible and physically dramatic.

lead_characters.name: Vivian
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16; popular, sexually confident, socially dominant teen.
lead_characters.hook: Vivian is the school’s fantasy object and social predator, all hair, cleavage, and contempt until the script reveals she is also a pact-made construct with her own bargain. She functions as both desire object and status weapon, which keeps her from being just a stock mean girl.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of glossy, dangerous teen role that made Rachel McAdams in Mean Girls a star-making presence — a character who can weaponize charm, cruelty, and status in the same scene. It gives an actor a high-visibility, high-quote role with instant poster value.

lead_characters.name: Wayne
lead_characters.hook: Wayne is Leo’s straight-man friend, but the script lets him be more than a tagalong by making him the skeptical voice and later revealing his own sexual truth. He has the best deadpan friction in the buddy trio and quietly becomes one of the story’s more surprising emotional turns.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of comic-support role that gave Seth Rogen in Freaks and Geeks or Michael Cera in early ensemble comedy real scene-stealing territory — dry, reactive, and memorable. It offers an actor a chance to play understatement inside a very loud movie.

lead_characters.name: Bruce
lead_characters.hook: Bruce is the most openly absurd of Leo’s friends, a weed-and-gag machine who helps keep the movie in motion and gives the trio its loose, juvenile chemistry. He’s less emotionally complicated than Wayne, but he’s a reliable comic pressure valve.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of broad best-friend role that lets an actor do timing, reaction, and physical comedy in a way that can become a calling card. It’s the sort of part that can break out if played with precision rather than just volume.

lead_characters.name: God
lead_characters.hook: God is not a serene authority figure here but a blunt, profane negotiator with a bruised ego and a very human temper. The script makes him funny by making him petty, which is the movie’s most provocative theological choice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of voice role/performance territory that gave Morgan Freeman in Bruce Almighty or Alanis Morissette in Dogma a memorable pop-cultural afterlife — a divine figure with attitude. It gives an actor a chance to play authority as comedy.

lead_characters.name: Satan
lead_characters.hook: Satan is the movie’s true engine: seductive, argumentative, childish, and weirdly sincere about his pitch. He shifts from cute to monstrous to absurdly charming, which makes him feel like a comic antagonist and a co-host of the movie’s worldview.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-chewing role that gave Al Pacino in The Devil’s Advocate or John Lithgow in Raising Cain a chance to dominate every entrance. It’s a performance playground for an actor who can sell menace, wit, and absurdity at once.

lead_characters.name: Old Leo
lead_characters.hook: Old Leo is the bookend version of the protagonist, using his deathbed to force the family to hear the story he thinks matters most. He gives the script its framing device and its final ironic distance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of elder-storyteller role that gives an actor gravitas, comic timing, and a late-scene reveal of emotional purpose. It’s a compact but memorable framing part.

lead_characters.name: Bert
lead_characters.hook: Bert is one of the impatient adult sons who treats the deathbed story like an inconvenience, which makes him the audience’s built-in skeptic. He’s less a full arc than a pressure point for the framing device.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean character-actor role — the kind of part that lets an actor play irritation, entitlement, and family fatigue in a few sharp scenes.

lead_characters.name: Dave
lead_characters.hook: Dave is another skeptical son, functioning as a comic adult foil to Old Leo’s insistence on telling the story. He helps establish the family’s emotional distance and the story’s generational irony.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor a few strong reaction beats and a clear family dynamic to play against.

lead_characters.name: Thomas
lead_characters.hook: Thomas is the youngest of the adult sons and arguably the most openly contemptuous, which sharpens the family’s dysfunction. He’s a useful antagonist inside the framing scene, even if the script keeps him broad.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, scene-specific role for an actor who can land sarcasm and impatience quickly.

lead_characters.name: Theodore
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 15; Leo’s grandson; teen with colorful rapper style.
lead_characters.hook: Theodore is the disengaged teen in the deathbed frame, the one who seems least interested in the story but ends up being the only one who appreciates it. He gives the ending a small but effective generational wink.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a light but memorable teen role with a distinct visual profile and a final payoff beat.

lead_characters.name: Arnold
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens; muscular popular teen.
lead_characters.hook: Arnold is the alpha-party host and physical embodiment of the school hierarchy Leo wants to enter. He’s broad, dominant, and eventually cruel, which makes him the story’s most immediate human obstacle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bully/heartthrob role that gives an actor a strong physical presence and a clear social power dynamic to play.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best positioned for a cult-leaning streaming launch or specialty theatrical play rather than broad theatrical.

budget.note: Contemporary teen settings keep the base footprint manageable, but the God/Satan transformations, white-void/hell sequences, and room-collapse effects push this beyond a simple contained comedy.

casting.note: The project needs a lead who can play horny, pathetic, funny, and sincere without losing audience sympathy, plus a blind teen role, a muscular teen bully, and older framing roles across three generations.

development.note: The concept is clear, but the script’s reliance on repeated temptation dialogue, broad shock comedy, and a very specific blasphemous register will require a buyer aligned to that exact tone.

comp_set.title: American Pie
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the horny-teen POV, humiliation comedy, and coming-of-age sexual panic that drives the lead’s engine.

comp_set.title: Dogma
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the irreverent theology, profane divine dialogue, and comic treatment of heaven/hell as argumentative characters.

comp_set.title: Bruce Almighty
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the premise of a mortal negotiating directly with God for personal desire, with comedy built from divine intervention.

comp_set.title: Mean Girls
comp_set.why_it_comps: The school hierarchy, popular-girl cruelty, and social-status obsession give it a similar teen ecosystem.

comp_set.title: The Devil's Advocate
comp_set.why_it_comps: The seductive, manipulative Satan figure and the bargain-with-the-devil structure echo the film’s central temptation dynamic.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like raunchy, irreverent genre comedies and cult-friendly teen nostalgia.
audience_target.demographics: 18-34 skew with male tilt, but with a secondary 35+ cult-comedy audience; strongest with viewers comfortable with explicit sexual humor and blasphemous satire.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary teen interiors, one major party set-piece, and moderate fantasy VFX keep this in indie feature territory, though the hell/void effects and ensemble party coverage add scope.

types_of_buyers: indie financiers chasing cult breakout potential
director-driven buyers with a taste for irreverent high-concept material
lane_fit.detail: The script sits in a lane where explicit teen comedy meets supernatural satire, which is a recognizable cult proposition if packaged with the right comic lead and a director who can control the chaos.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed bargain story and no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the central Leo/Amanda/Satan premise.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hook is immediate and pitchable.
strengths.what_it_means: A buyer can understand the movie in one sentence, which helps it travel fast in a room and makes it easy to market as a high-concept comedy-fantasy. That clarity is attractive to streamer comedy buyers and indie financiers looking for a clean hook.
strengths.evidence: Leo prays for Vivian, God appears, Satan appears, and the story becomes a bargain over love, status, and soul ownership.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The theology is profane and ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: God and Satan are not abstract symbols here; they are comic characters with voices, tempers, and agendas, which gives the script a distinct brand. That kind of irreverent mythology is catnip for buyers seeking cult-friendly genre comedy with a clear point of view.
strengths.evidence: The God/Satan conversations, the “panda in Taiwan” bit, and the repeated bargaining over souls give the movie its signature comic texture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Leo is a playable comic lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role offers a young actor humiliation comedy, sexual panic, stoner banter, and a late emotional pivot, which is exactly the kind of part that can launch a breakout. Casting a lead who can make self-loathing funny without losing sympathy is a real asset in this lane.
strengths.evidence: Leo’s prayer scene, his party humiliation, and his eventual choice to help Amanda all show a lead who can carry both broad jokes and a sincere turn.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The party sequence gives the movie a set-piece engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The Arnold house party functions as a contained escalation chamber where every social hierarchy in the script can collide, which is efficient for production and strong for audience momentum. Buyers like a movie that can promise one big, messy, memorable set-piece without needing a giant world build.
strengths.evidence: The beer run, the drug dealer exchange, the basement fort, the cow in the living room, and the final public humiliation all happen inside one party ecosystem.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Amanda gives the ending emotional lift.
strengths.what_it_means: The blind-girl-to-seeing-girl transformation creates a late emotional reversal that broadens the movie beyond pure shock comedy. That makes the script more attractive to buyers who want a cult premise with a human payoff, not just a string of gags.
strengths.evidence: Leo restores Amanda’s sight, she recognizes the world, and then she punches Vivian before kissing Leo.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept cult-comedy package: a horny teen bargain with God and Satan, a lead role built for humiliation-to-heartbreak comedy, and a contained party-set production footprint that keeps the economics sane. The irreverent theology and teen hierarchy give it a distinct lane for streamer or specialty buyers who want something loud, quotable, and easy to pitch.

items.area: The script leans hard on shock over escalation.
items.detail: A lot of the middle is built from repeated sexual gags, profanity, and humiliation beats rather than new turns in the bargain engine. That keeps the tone loud, but it also means the movie’s momentum depends on whether a buyer wants this exact register for a full feature.

Several Satan/God exchanges explain the rules at length, especially in the bathroom and locker-room sequences. The premise is clear, but the script spends a lot of time restating the bargain mechanics instead of letting the scenes turn on action.

The script uses slurs, sexual humiliation, disability jokes, and blasphemy as part of its comic identity. That is a real lane, but it narrows the buyer pool to audiences and platforms comfortable with a very aggressive, non-family tone.

items.area: The supporting cast is vivid but broad.
items.detail: Vivian, Arnold, Wayne, Bruce, and the party crowd all have strong surface color, but most of them function as social types rather than deeply layered engines. That makes the movie easy to read quickly, but it limits the depth buyers will expect from the ensemble.

issues.headline: The main friction is tonal and structural: the movie knows exactly how outrageous it wants to be, but it often repeats the same joke shape while explaining the rules of the bargain. Buyers will also clock the aggressive content level immediately, which makes this a targeted cult play rather than a broad commercial comedy.
